paper_title: EMBER: Predicting TCR--pMHC Binding Without a Docked Complex

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We propose EMBER, a structure-based framework for TCR--pMHC binding prediction that eliminates the need for a predicted docked complex, and with it the placement error that dominates such predictions. Traditional structure-based predictors utilize the co-folded complex structure of the receptor and the antigen and interpret binding from its contact surface. Consequently, every downstream feature inherits any deviation the structure-prediction tool introduced. Methodologically, EMBER folds the TCR and pMHC independently, encodes them as SE(3)-invariant residue graphs, and compares their learned representations without constructing a shared coordinate frame. A relative pose is therefore not an input of the model, so placement error cannot propagate into the prediction. Computationally, EMBER preprocesses $O(N{+}M)$ monomer folds where a complex-based predictor needs $O(NM)$ operations. Experimentally, under epitope-disjoint evaluation with six retrained baselines, EMBER is first on every metric under all four folding tools, by 0.9 to 14.4% in micro-AUROC, 18.5 to 25.3% in micro-AUPRC and 10.6 to 24.1% in MCC. Its ranking is also up to 85% more stable across folding tools.

sections.title:
1
We propose EMBER, a structure-based predictor of TCR–pMHC binding that never forms a docked complex.
It folds each molecule once as an unbound monomer, encodes the two independently, and scores the pair by
comparing SE(3)-invariant descriptors, so the relative pose of the two molecules never enters the computation.
Because TCR–pMHC binding determines adaptive immune specificity [11] while the candidate space is far
too large for exhaustive experimental screening, EMBER provides a scalable way to prioritize likely binders,
including for unseen epitopes.
sections.content: Existing structure-based TCRpMHC predictors make this decision through predicted docked complex, first folding or docking the two molecules into common assembly and then inferring binding from the predicted interface, using residue contacts, geometric features, or structure-derived graphs [2, 22, 30, 3537]. The design follows the biology, since recognition happens at the interface and sequence alone does not explain specificity [11, 19]. However, it also makes the downstream predictor dependent on the accuracy of the upstream complex prediction. In particular, these methods typically retain only residues within fixed distance of the opposing molecule [2, 22, 36]. The predicted relative pose therefore determines not only the geometric 1 features presented to the model, but also which residues and intermolecular contacts exist in its input graph. An error in rigid-body placement can thus change the input itself, rather than merely perturb its coordinates. Although Polster et al. [30] attribute their models limitations to structural prediction error, whether predicted TCRpMHC complexes are reliable in these task-critical quantities has not been systematically tested. Figure 1 Three routes to binding prediction. All methods score the same molecular pair. Sequence-based methods use no structural information; structure-based methods dock the molecules and construct joint interface graph with pose-dependent contacts; EMBER instead folds each molecule independently and connects the two monomer graphs only through attention. To address this limitation, we propose EMBER, which removes complex assembly rather than correcting its errors. Each molecule is folded as an unbound monomer and represented as residue graph, with Cαcentered nodes carrying local geometric descriptors and cached protein language-model embeddings. Edges connect nearest neighbors and encode spatial separation and biochemical compatibility. Because all input features are invariant to rigid-body transformations, no absolute coordinates or inter-molecular pose enter the representation. Given these pose-independent graphs, shared equivariant encoder processes the two molecules separately, restricting message passing to within each molecule and updating neighborhoods from the evolving coordinates at each layer. Cross-molecule interaction occurs only through bidirectional attention between the CDR3 loops and peptide, whose residue sets are defined by sequence annotation rather than predicted geometry. Thus, EMBER neither constructs shared coordinate frame nor selects residues using inter-molecular distance cutoffs. Pose independence is therefore imposed by the model architecture and is preserved throughout training. Contributions. We present EMBER (Figure 1), monomer-only TCRpMHC structure-based predictor which is provably independent of the relative pose of the two molecules. Our main contributions are: We identify assembly-induced interface corruption (AIC), previously uncharacterized failure mode in structure-based TCRpMHC prediction, where pose errors corrupt the residues and contacts exposed to downstream predictors. We propose EMBER, pose-free structure-based predictor that folds the TCR and pMHC independently as unbound monomers. Each molecule is encoded as an SE(3)-invariant residue graph with shared encoder, and binding is scored by bidirectional attention over the resulting representations. EMBER preprocesses O(N +M ) monomer folds, against the O(N ) complex predictions complex-based predictor needs. Experimentally, EMBER leads six published baselines retrained on identical data and splits, first on every metric under all four folding tools. It is also significantly more stable to the choice of folding tool.

sections.title:
2 Related Work
Existing approaches to TCR–pMHC binding prediction fall broadly into sequence-based and structure-
informed families. Sequence models, including NetTCR [13, 27] and ERGO-II [38], learn directly from
amino-acid sequences and benefit from substantially larger sequence datasets than are available for solved
TCR–pMHC complexes [20, 34, 43]. However, recent benchmarking and systematic evaluation show that
generalization to unseen epitopes remains limited [9, 24]. TEIM predicts the residue contacts themselves
from sequence and HeteroTCR builds a heterogeneous graph over sequence embeddings, so neither reads
a structure [29, 46]. Advances in protein structure prediction enabled a second family of methods that
incorporates predicted three-dimensional structure [3, 15]. Most construct a predicted TCR–pMHC complex
and infer binding from its interface using residue contacts, geometric features, and graph representations
[5, 22, 30, 35–37]. These methods typically define the interface by a distance cutoff of 8 to 14 Å, so the
predicted pose determines not only residue geometry but also which residues and intermolecular contacts
enter the model. Other approaches reduce this dependence by using the structure of only one binding partner
[12, 14, 33, 47] or by using structure only during training [21], but do not exploit the structural information
of both molecules. Prior work has already reported unreliable docking confidence [8] and that non-interacting
complexes adopt conformations geometrically similar to interacting ones [31].
sections.content: EMBER occupies distinct point in this design space. STAG, SageTCR and the classifier of Abeer et al. [2] identify only the residues within 10 to 14 Å of the opposing molecule as the interface [22, 36]. STAG-LLM keeps every residue and wires the assembly with 10 Å radius graph [37], so there the pose decides the contacts rather than the residues. EMBER processes each monomer in full and links the two only through sequence-annotated residue sets, so neither choice is exposed to the pose. TRAP avoids the assembly by dropping the receptor structure and representing the TCR by sequence [12], while EMBER keeps the structure of both. caTCR [14] also folds its two inputs separately, though it folds only the CDR3β loop and the epitope and leaves the MHC out of the model. It reduces each to matrix of pairwise Cα distances and reads that matrix with convolutional network, whose neighborhoods follow the residue order rather than the spatial arrangement. EMBER carries coordinates as an equivariant field and updates them at every layer. Running an E(n)-equivariant network over the joint graph, as Abeer et al. [2] does, leaves the score invariant to motion of the whole assembly while the relative pose stays in the input. In contrast, EMBER removes the relative pose by Proposition 1.

sections.title:
3 Assembly-induced Interface Corruption
In this section, we test whether predicted TCR–pMHC complexes provide reliable structural inputs for
downstream binding prediction. We evaluate six co-folding tools on 49 class-I TCR–pMHC crystal structures
from STCRDab [20]. The tools are Boltz-2 [28], ESMFold2 [7], TCRmodel2 [45], AlphaFold-Multimer [10],
OpenDDE [4] and tFold-TCR [44]. We focus on two quantities consumed by structure-based predictors: the
intermolecular contacts at the interface and the relative placement of the two molecules.
sections.content: We term assembly-induced interface corruption (AIC) the failure mode in which rigid-body placement error changes the interface presented to the downstream model. Because traditional structure-based models construct interface graphs using distance cutoffs of 814 Å, an error of comparable magnitude can alter which residues and intermolecular contacts enter the graph, producing misleading information. In short, we found that no tool reconstructs the native interface reliably. Setting Boltz-2 aside, the median contact Jaccard at 5 Å runs from 0.188 to 0.459 and the median receptor Cα RMSD from 5.87 to 8.09 Å. Boltz-2 is best in almost every row and reaches Jaccard of 0.833, but 39 of the 49 targets were seen by it during training. On the 10 targets released after Boltz-2s training cutoff, its Jaccard falls from 0.833 to 0.155. The other five tools move far less on those same targets, ESMFold2 from 0.459 to 0.393 and AlphaFold-Multimer from 0.308 to 0.303. Therefore the lead of Boltz-2 reflects memorization rather than generalization ability. Table 8 and Table 9 list the details. More specifically, we locate the error in assembly rather than in monomer folding. Peptides remain close to their crystal positions, whereas CDR3 loops and the receptor as whole are displaced substantially further (Figure 2c). Across tools, receptor placements differ by 5.10 to 7.80 Å on the same complexes, while independently folded TCR monomers agree to within 0.96 to 1.23 Å over the same 250 TCR monomers (Figure 2d). sections.title:
5 Experiments
We evaluate EMBER against six published baselines on a curated set of four public datasets, over five
epitope-disjoint folds and three seeds.
sections.content: Dataset. We utilize four public datasetsMcPAS-TCR, VDJdb, IEDB, and 10x Genomicscovering 45,909 TCRpMHC pairs across 343 epitopes [1, 34, 40, 43]. Following Slone et al. [36], 7,371 measured binders are augmented with sampled non-binders, yielding binder prevalence of 0.161. Baselines. To evaluate EMBER against diverse TCRpMHC predictors, we compare with six baselines spanning three structural, one hybrid, and two sequence-based methods. Structural baselines include STAGLLM [37], SageTCR [22], and the dual-encoder classifier of Abeer et al. [2]; TRAP [12] combines pMHC structure with TCR sequence, whereas NetTCR-2.2 [13] and ERGO-II [38] read no structure. We retrain each method using its published hyperparameters across five folds and three random seeds, reporting means over all 15 runs and standard deviations across seeds. Metrics. To evaluate the performance of EMBER, we measure ranking quality, classification accuracy, and cross-tool stability. Ranking is assessed by microand macro-averaged AUROC and AUPRC; classification uses MCC at fixed threshold of 0.5, reported alongside MCC at the threshold that maximizes it on the test fold, which no deployed system has and which we report only to bound what threshold tuning could buy baseline. Stability is quantified by pairwise Kendalls τb, Kendalls concordance across all four folding tools, and Overlap@k between top-ranked candidates. Section F.2 provides the definitions.

sections.title:
5.1 Binding Prediction and Stability against Retrained Baselines
We conduct experiments on five epitope-disjoint folds, ensuring that all test peptides are unseen during
training. We run the comparison on structures generated by four different tools, retraining every method on
that tool’s structures (Table 1 and Figure 4). A structure-based predictor inherits its upstream tool, and the
folding tools disagree, so we also measure how far that choice moves the answer. For each epitope and fold we
rank that epitope’s candidate TCRs with the same method trained on each tool’s structures, then compare
the rankings (Table 2).
Results. EMBER is first on every metric under every folding tool, and the size of the lead depends on which
part of the ranking a metric reads. AUROC weighs the whole candidate list, and there the strongest baseline
comes close. STAG-LLM trails EMBER by 0.011 in micro-AUROC under ESMFold2 and by 0.006 under
Boltz-2, so the whole-list metric barely separates the two. Metrics that weigh the top of the list give a different
reading. On micro-AUPRC the same baseline trails by 0.058 to 0.074, and on MCC at a fixed threshold of 0.5
it trails by 51 to 75%. Calibration accounts for part of that last figure, since tuning the threshold on the
test fold narrows the lead to 10 to 24%. What remains after the tuning is discrimination, and a deployed
screen meets both terms at once, because it reads the top of the list at a threshold fixed in advance. Read
one fold at a time, the lead holds on all five folds in 16 of the 24 cells, and the eight that fall short are two
micro-AUROC cells, two micro-AUPRC cells and all four MCC∗ cells (Table 15).

5.2 Influence of Structure
We conduct three analyses to assess how structural information influences prediction. First, we directly use
each folding tool’s interface confidence as a training-free binding score. Second, we stratify co-folded pairs
into confidence percentile bands and evaluate each method at its own operating threshold (Figure 5); because

sections.title:
6 Conclusion
We propose EMBER, a pose-independent framework for TCR–pMHC binding prediction that avoids assembly-
induced interface corruption (AIC), a failure mode in which complex-placement errors alter the residues and
contacts presented to downstream predictors. Testing across 49 crystal structures on six folding tools, we
show that such placement errors are substantial. By encoding each molecule independently, EMBER removes
relative pose from the binding score and is first on every metric under all four folding tools, improving MCC
at the fixed threshold of 0.5 by 51 to 75% over the strongest baseline and ranking stability across folding
tools by 26 to 85% over structural baselines. It also cuts preprocessing by up to 19.4× on the same evaluation
set. These results suggest a different way of using predicted structure for the TCR–pMHC prediction task.
EMBER uses only the trustworthy part of TCR and pMHC structures, and it is both more accurate and
more stable for it.
